### [00:11:14.860 - 00:11:21.860]

And at a very high level can basically classify NLP tasks into three buckets.

### [00:11:21.860 - 00:11:25.860]

So the first buckets is what we call classification.

### [00:11:25.860 - 00:11:29.860]

So we have an input text as an inputs.

And then what we want is to predict something.

So one example is you have a movie review and you want to predict whether, uh, the sentiment is positive, negative, or neutral.

### [00:11:42.860 - 00:11:44.860]

### [00:11:44.860 - 00:11:47.860]

### [00:11:47.860 - 00:11:50.860]

So let's suppose you say, I want to create an alarm for tomorrow.

### [00:11:54.860 - 00:11:57.860]

So the intent here is create an alarm.

So also to detect the language.

So for instance, if you write a more in French, you want to detect that that text is in French.

Topic modeling.

### [00:12:09.860 - 00:12:13.860]

The second category is what we call multi classification.

### [00:12:13.860 - 00:12:20.860]

So we still have a text as inputs, but this time we predict more than one thing.

### [00:12:20.860 - 00:12:24.860]

So you have a number of tasks in that bucket as well.

### [00:12:24.860 - 00:12:31.860]

So one that is very popular is called named entity recognition, AKA NER.

### [00:12:31.860 - 00:12:39.860]

So what that task does is given an input text, we want to basically label some specific words.

### [00:12:39.860 - 00:12:46.860]

Like for instance, identifying whether something is a location or a time and so on.

### [00:12:46.860 - 00:12:52.860]

And then you have some other tasks as well that are a little bit more on the linguistic side.

### [00:14:32.860 - 00:14:37.860]

Let's suppose we have a sentence, this teddy bear is so cute.

We want our model to predict, you know, this to be a positive sentiment.

### [00:14:42.860 - 00:14:47.860]

Typically what you would use is, you know, data sets that are around, you know, sentiment extraction data sets.

### [00:14:47.860 - 00:14:49.860]

So I mentioned movie reviews.

### [00:14:49.860 - 00:14:57.860]

So this is IMDB critics, but you also have reviews about products, Amazon reviews or, you know, tweets.

### [00:15:01.860 - 00:15:11.860]

And the way you would evaluate such outputs would be by typically using traditional classification metrics.

### [00:15:11.860 - 00:15:18.860]

So you have accuracy, which is, you know, how many, what is the percentage of the observations that you correctly predicted.

### [00:15:18.860 - 00:15:24.860]

But you also have two key metrics, which I'm just going to remind.

### [00:15:24.860 - 00:15:26.860]

I'm not sure if everyone knows about them.

### [00:15:26.860 - 00:15:36.860]

So one is precision, which is out of all the positive predictions that you made, which ones were correct.

### [00:15:36.860 - 00:15:39.860]

And then the second one is recall.

### [00:15:39.860 - 00:15:46.860]

Out of all the true labels, how many of them did you correctly predict as being positive?

### [00:15:46.860 - 00:15:55.860]

And you have this metric called the F1 score, which basically takes the harmonic mean of precision and recall to just give you one number.

### [00:15:55.860 - 00:16:00.860]

So now you may wonder, you know, why do you need all these metrics?

### [00:16:00.860 - 00:16:09.860]

So the short answer is that sometimes you have tasks and data sets where your classes are very imbalanced.

### [00:16:09.860 - 00:16:18.860]

So for instance, you can have 99% of your data set that is a positive label and then only 1% of the data set, which is negative.

### [00:16:18.860 - 00:16:31.860]

And so here, if you take like a metric like accuracy, it would be very misleading because if you have a model that would predict everything as the majority class,

### [00:16:31.860 - 00:16:35.860]

then you would have a great classifier, but that's not the case.

### [00:16:35.860 - 00:16:40.860]

So that's why precision and recall really play a role.

So that's sort of the first one.
